cards.title: Colorado River Allocation
cards.script:
![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787850366846-c3j9.png)

Is capitalism to blame for the overuse of the Colorado River?

Afterall, the most profitable use for water is extraction.

Golf courses in the desert. High rise condos. Sprawling Metropolises.

However, there's just one problem with this narrative - The Colorado River is not run by the unadulterated free market.

It's central planning with feudal characteristics.

Here's what I mean.

1. There's no real functioning water market.  I mean, yes, there's some markets for temporary leasing inside of California, but these don't really last more than a year or two. You can't plan big long-term projects like that. This prevents it from going to its highest value.

The government decided 150 years ago how much water a particular plot of land can extract. And those - now practically ancient - water claims keep getting past down from generation to generation like the feudal lords of old.

2. Unlike other assets in capitalism, it's use it or lose it. No incentive for thriftiness, savings, or storing for the future.

Result: the classic soviet-style waste you get from central planning.

But wait, why aren't the big cities and the 40 million people relying on the Colorado River the real ones to blame?

This graph looks at where all the water comes from - and where it goes.

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787843787982-roqu.png)

Most the water enters in the Upper Basin largely through snowmelt from the Rockies.

Now, look at MCI: Municipal, Commercial, and Industrial use. It's a very small share compared to agriculture. And that agriculture is largely devoted to growing Alfalfa and Hay, an incredibly low-value cash crop.

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787850314567-m1k6.png)

When we look at the Great Salt Lake basin, we also see a similar result. The usable water goes to alfalfa businesses, not homes.

And of course, The Salt Lake experiences a lot of evaporation - it's shallow and spread out.

How bad is the problem? The Salt Lake is declining every decade. Lakes Powell and Mead are now near record lows.

It's estimated that we need to reduce water use by 3 million acre-feet or by a 25% just to stabilize the reservoirs, And even more by 2050 as climate warming continues to reduce runoff.

So, where should the cuts happen?

If you ask an economist - we'd say the activity that brings the least value.

What is the best way to determine this? Create a market.

We've already successfully done this. It's how we solved the Acid Rain problem back in the 90's.

We need a cap and trade for the Colorado River.

A functioning water market would allocated it to our most valuable purpose. Today, farmers profits are boosted on the backs of working families. Farmers pay on avg $30 per acre foot compared to the $512 dollars the rest of us pay.

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787839527433-2ecs.jpg)

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787839529928-4pt1.jpg)

Yeah, you give me a bunch of free stuff, you bet I'll turn a profit.

We call this rent seeking. Earning profits not because you produce what society values most, but because you force society to pay you more than what you produce. These are inefficient cash crops.

In The Great Salt Lake Basin, hay and alfalfa only contribute 0.07% to the economy. Did you see how many zeros there are, there?! Not just less than 1%, less than 0.1%.

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787849129557-detv.jpg)

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787849131550-qpuw.jpg)

How expensive would it be to just pay the farmers off? Only about $100 a year to save to Salt Lake, less than an annual Netflix subscription. But I gotta be honest, it's sits uneasy to me that in perpetuity, passed onto generations, farmers and their descendants get free cash from the public, just cuz of some great great grandad.

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787849133071-jrkt.jpg)

The economics can work here, if we choose it. As the authors note, the debate about whether to save the Great Salt Lake is about cultural issues, not economics or food security. It's the lifestyles of the 20k farmers and ranchers in the basin. That is - in a region of 2.8M, we are going to give out cultural sympathy points to businesses that produce a low value product?

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787849134938-vvr4.jpg)

That ain't capitalism.

Look, the cradle of modern civilization was built by large scale canals in Mesopotamia 6k years ago. Humanity created its very first government to cooperate in building larger economic possibilities.

![[Allen, Bertrazzini, & Heldring (2024) The Economic Origins of Government. AER](https://www.aeaweb.org/research/economic-origins-government-iraq)](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787854798345-qnvr.jpg)

So, too, today, can we use government to  limit our scarce western water, while allowing well regulated markets to allocate it to its most prosperous use.

We need more well regulated water markets, not historical feudal water claims. The Salt Lake and Colorado River Basins can support cities two or even three times as large, doubling the economy. All while preserving even more water reserves for wet lands and environmental needs.
